issues.legal_issue: A court deciding a summary application for possession pending final determination of succession rights cannot conclusively determine the validity of a disputed will or title to the property.
material_facts: The application sought possession under the statutory procedure for protecting a deceased person’s property.
The opposing claimant relied on a disputed joint will to claim possession.
The court conducted a detailed examination of the will and conclusively found it genuine, then relied on that finding to award possession.
Earlier orders had directed that the will’s genuineness be established in a regular suit.
issues.conclusion: The detailed and conclusive determination of the will’s genuineness was beyond the scope of the summary proceeding; that issue had to be determined in an appropriate regular suit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 192–195 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 provide for interlocutory, summary proceedings to determine who should hold possession pending final determination of the parties’ rights. Sections 208 and 209 preserve a regular suit to establish title and make clear that a summary decision settles actual possession only. A will may be considered in the summary proceeding to some extent, as recognized in Clarence Pais v. Union of India, but its validity cannot be determined conclusively through detailed adjudication there.

predicates.summary_succession_possession_proceeding: A person invoked a summary proceeding to obtain possession of property left by a deceased person pending final determination of succession rights.
predicates.disputed_will_used_to_claim_possession: A person opposing the possession claim relied on a disputed will as the basis for claiming possession.
predicates.court_made_detailed_conclusive_finding_o: The court examined the will in detail and conclusively determined its validity in the summary proceeding.

issues.definition: When a summary possession court makes a detailed and conclusive finding about a disputed will used to claim possession, the will’s validity must instead be decided in a regular suit.

issues.legal_issue: A summary possession court cannot award an entire property to one claimant on a disputed title claim while excluding another claimant whose share is undisputed.
material_facts: One claimant’s right to half of the property was undisputed.
The opposing claimant asserted a right to the property under a disputed will.
The court awarded possession of the entire property to the opposing claimant based on its finding about the will.
issues.conclusion: Possession was to be delivered to the claimant whose half share was undisputed, pending final adjudication of the disputed rights; the claim for mesne profits was to be deposited in court pending that adjudication.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 192–195 and 209 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, the summary proceeding determines actual possession pending a regular suit and does not finally settle title. A court exercising that jurisdiction cannot use a disputed title claim to exclude a person whose share is beyond controversy. The eventual determination of disputed title and mesne profits belongs in the appropriate proceeding.

predicates.summary_succession_possession_proceeding: A person invoked a summary proceeding to determine possession of a deceased person’s property pending final adjudication of rights.
predicates.claimant_has_undisputed_share: A claimant’s share in the property is accepted as beyond dispute.
predicates.whole_property_awarded_to_rival_on_dispu: The court gave the entire property to another claimant based on a contested claim of title.

issues.definition: If an entire property is awarded on a disputed title claim in a summary possession proceeding despite another claimant having an undisputed share, possession must be delivered to that sharer pending final adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court cannot refuse to correct a grave illegality in a summary possession order merely by treating interference as discretionary.
material_facts: The lower court conclusively adjudicated the validity of a disputed will in a summary possession proceeding and awarded the whole property to the opposing claimant.
The reviewing court recognized that the opposing claimant’s rights should be determined in an appropriate proceeding but dismissed the challenge as a matter of discretion.
The excluded claimant had an undisputed share in the property and had objected to adjudication of the will in the summary proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to interfere was set aside because the lower court’s excess of jurisdiction and resulting exclusion of the undisputed sharer constituted grave illegality.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial discretion must be exercised according to law and established principles, not arbitrarily or by whim. Sharp v. Wakefield and S.G. Jaisinghani v. Union of India support the requirement that discretion be regulated by law; Lee v. Budge Railway Co. likewise describes discretion as judicial rather than capricious. A discretionary refusal to interfere does not excuse a grave illegality causing miscarriage of justice.

predicates.revision_against_summary_possession_orde: A party challenged by revision an order made in a summary proceeding determining possession of a deceased person’s property.
predicates.lower_court_committed_grave_jurisdiction: The lower court exceeded the permitted scope of the summary proceeding in a way that caused serious injustice.
predicates.reviewing_court_refused_interference_as_: The reviewing court declined to correct the order on the ground that interference was discretionary.

issues.definition: When a reviewing court declines to correct a grave jurisdictional illegality in a summary possession order by relying on discretion, that refusal must be set aside.
